newsitem.title: USA: This time around, Clinton may take flak on Medicare.
newsitem.headline: This time around, Clinton may take flak on Medicare.

text.p: President Bill Clinton may look forward to a swift, harmonious bipartisan accord on Medicare's financial woes next year but Republicans smarting over campaign "Medigoguery" may not be so eager to oblige.
Both parties recognize that Medicare's hospital trust fund is heading for bankruptcy around the year 2001.

For the most part, both sides also agree that at least some reforms must be made to the program overall to help balance the federal budget and ensure that Medicare can handle the baby boomers who start retiring around 2010.
But last year, the two parties could not agree on how much to restrain spending, or how to revamp the popular program, which covers 38 million elderly and disabled people.

They could not even agree to enact the parts they agreed on, and the stalemate over Medicare became emblematic of the bitter election-year struggle between the Democratic White House and an assertive Republican Congress.
All through the campaign, Democrats and their labor union allies hit the Republicans hard on Medicare, accusing them of wrecking or eviscerating it.
Those accusations went down well with elderly voters, and explain in large part why Florida backed a Democrat for the first time in 20 years, Arizona for the first time in 48.
The watchword since last week's election has been bipartisanship, and Clinton at his post-election news conference on Friday invited Congress to work with him.

"The way to put this (Medicare bitterness) behind us is reach an agreement. I'm prepared to reach out and meet them halfway," Clinton said, inviting congressional leaders to the White House to start talks next week.
But if Republicans are willing to call a truce on Whitewater and other partisan hot buttons, peacemaking might not be so easy on Medicare.

"The Democrats were promising voters not to make changes, and the Republicans were getting beaten up on for months for proposing changes. That does not make people want to belly up to the bar," said health policy analyst Gail Wilensky, a Republican who is pessimistic about anything significant getting done next year.

"It's relatively easy to do half the job," said economist Robert Reischauer, who directed the Congressional Budget Office under the Democrats. "But if you do that, the impetus for structural reform is going to dissipate rather rapidly."

The goal of the Democrats, several analysts said, is to get the less painful aspects of Medicare reform done quickly and to leave to a bipartisan commission the more politically treacherous aspects, including changes that could boost the charges to patients or limit their choices and coverage.
They could also be helped if, as some experts expect, the December budget figures show Medicare spending is slower than had been forecast even without wholesale reform.
The goal of the Republicans, the analysts said, is to get bigger reforms through soon -- but make sure the head on the chopping block is Clinton's and not one of their own.

"We are going to have to make changes in these programs. But it is now the president who is going to have to sell these programs," California Republican Bill Thomas, who chairs the House Health subcommittee that oversees Medicare, told a business audience the other day in a speech sharply critical of Clinton and Democratic "Medigoguery."

"My lament is over the fact that it's now going to be more difficult to do what we have to do. The reason it's more difficult is because of the Medigoguery the president to the last minute engaged in," Thomas added.

According to the Democrats, the two sides agree on about $90-$100 billion of savings. Republicans scoff at that, saying the Democrats are using accounting gimmicks and the actual areas of agreement are much narrower.

Changes to the program could involve many politically unpopular steps such as raising the premiums and co-payments that patients pay, adding incentives to go into managed care, raising the age of eligibility from 65 to 67 or even older, or reducing the health services covered.

Easier, politically, is slowing payments to doctors, hospitals and other healthcare providers, who anticipate cuts and have maneuvered for various antitrust, legal or insurance reforms to soften the blow.

"Do you really even need a commission for restructuring," said Tom Scully, who heads a federation of for-profit hospitals. "You can probably work it out in a week, most people know what's going on, it's not rocket science."
"It's not the policy issues that are so tough. It's the politics."
